extraction.name: LAMBADA
extraction.description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word.
extraction.creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Passages were extracted from the Book Corpus and pre-filtered using a combination of four language models to remove passages where the target word had probability >= 0.00175. A random sample of the remaining passages was evaluated by human subjects through CrowdFlower in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; (2) if correct, a second subject guessed based on the whole passage; (3) if also correct, more subjects (up to 10) tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only (with 3 guesses allowed per sentence). Passages were included only if both broad-context subjects guessed the exact word and no subject guessed it from the target sentence alone.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), containing unpublished novels.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material using a stop word list. Passages were composed of a context (minimum complete sentences containing at least 50 tokens, averaging 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence whose last word is the target. The corpus was randomly split by novels into training and dev+test partitions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdsourced human word-guessing task conducted in three steps: Step 1 required one human rater to guess the missing target word given the entire passage; Step 2 required a second human rater to also correctly guess the missing word given the passage; Step 3 required raters to guess the missing word given only the target sentence (allowed 3 guesses per sentence, up to 10 unsuccessful subjects). Only passages where steps 1 and 2 yielded exact matches and step 3 yielded zero correct guesses were retained.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Criteria were strict hit-or-miss: exact matching of the original target word was required by two consecutive broad-context raters, and exactly zero raters (out of up to 10) could guess it from the target sentence alone, to unambiguously distinguish items solvable only in broad discourse context.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Between 3 and 12 subjects depending on the filtering step (2 broad-context subjects and up to 10 sentence-only subjects).
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: English speakers (subjects were paid $0.22 per page in steps 1 and 2, and $0.15 per page in step 3).
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: A pre-trained recurrent neural network (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three language models trained on the Book Corpus (standard 4-gram, RNN, and feed-forward model) used to filter out easy passages.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Proper nouns are heavily over-represented (48% of target words in LAMBADA), followed by common nouns (37%), whereas verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are rare. More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the preceding context. LAMBADA items also contain quoted direct speech significantly more often (71%) than the input items (61%).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Standard language models are bound to fail on LAMBADA by design because passages predictable by simple language models were filtered out. Filtering based on exact lexical matches excluded valid synonyms or plausible continuations.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning (development set can be used to fine-tune models, test set used to evaluate broad discourse context text understanding in language models; not intended as training data to develop ad-hoc target-word guessing models).
